title: AI Agents Open 40% of GitHub PRs, Up from 17% in March
summary: Microsoft's Copilot exec reveals AI agents initiated 40% of GitHub's 110M pull requests by September 2026, driving 14x workload surge as agents become
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- AI agents initiated over 40% of GitHub's 110 million pull requests by September 2026, jumping from 17% in March.
- GitHub experienced a 14x workload increase driven by agent activity, not human developer growth, according to Microsoft's Copilot executive.
- Microsoft is redesigning APIs and user experiences to serve agents as the dominant software users, reshaping enterprise workflows.


Microsoft's Charles Lamanna, Executive Vice President of Copilot, Agents and Platform, revealed that[AI agents](https://emergent.sh/ai-crm-builder/agents) initiated more than 40% of GitHub pull requests by September 2026, a dramatic jump from 17% in March. With approximately 110 million PRs opened during that period, the shift marks a fundamental change in how software is developed, tested, and deployed at scale. GitHub's workload surged 14x on the back of agent activity, a growth rate Lamanna attributes entirely to non-human contributors.


Officially launched on November 24, 2026, these findings align with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's recent statement that 20 million AI agents now operate alongside the company's workforce. The data, surfaced in GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report, underscores a broader industry trend: agents are transitioning from experimental tools to primary users of enterprise platforms.


## Agents as the Dominant Software Users


Lamanna frames the shift as inevitable. "I think it's probably inevitable that the main client of a lot of software and technology will be agents as we go forward," he told former Microsoft engineer Peter Yang in a recent interview. The executive already relies on Copilot Cowork agents for GPU capacity reviews and budget planning, treating them as first-class collaborators rather than assistants.


Unlike human users, agents demand maximum performance and programmability, often preferring data structures humans would find overwhelming. Lamanna's example: search results. Where a person benefits from 10 curated links, an agent can process thousands of results without fatigue. Microsoft is now redesigning APIs and user experiences to accommodate agent-first workflows, introducing modes optimized for machine consumption rather than human readability.


## GitHub's 14x Workload Surge


The 14x increase in GitHub's load is not driven by an equivalent rise in human developers. Instead, agents are filing issues, opening pull requests, running tests, and merging code at machine speed. By September 2026, 40% of the platform's 110 million PRs originated from automated systems, reflecting a 135% increase from the 17% share recorded in March.


Lamanna describes agents as "very harsh customers" who will abandon poorly performing systems without hesitation. Where a frustrated human user might complain and continue using a service, an agent simply stops sending requests. This behavior is forcing platform teams to prioritize latency, error handling, and API reliability in ways that human-centric design often overlooked.


## Rethinking Developer Workflows


As agents handle more code generation, Microsoft's engineering teams are shifting focus from line-by-line implementation to system design, verification, and safe rollouts. Lamanna's most "AI-pilled" teams no longer craft code manually but instead obsess over architecture, testing strategies, and coordination. "I feel like I've never had to think harder than I do right now," he said, comparing the transition to the leap from assembly language to compilers.


The executive acknowledges the tension. Critics point out that compilers never hallucinated incorrect migrations or dropped production databases, risks that remain present with large language models. Microsoft has admitted multiple times that AI agents can produce erroneous outputs, leaving engineers responsible for verification, a task that absorbs the time saved on coding.


## Copilot Workspaces and Enterprise Coordination


To address the isolation of single-player coding workflows, Microsoft introduced Copilot Workspaces at its Ignite conference last week. The feature suggests relevant people and agents to include when preparing customer proposals or managing supply chain disruptions, mirroring the collaborative nature of sales and finance teams. Lamanna argues that software engineering has "overfit" to solitary workflows, a model poorly suited to other knowledge work disciplines.


Despite integrating Word, Excel, and PowerPoint into the Copilot app, Lamanna insists the traditional Office suite remains essential. "I wanna move a text box eight pixels to the left, I just wanna click and drag," he said, rejecting the notion that conversational interfaces will replace direct manipulation tools. The Copilot platform serves as an orchestration layer, not a replacement for specialized applications.


## AI Etiquette and Output Volume


Lamanna also addressed workplace AI etiquette, warning against generating excessive content. "If you can't be bothered to say write 10 pages, you probably shouldn't generate 10 pages and send it to 10 people," he said, advocating for restraint in automated output. The executive writes a 20-page strategic memo every six months and relies on A/B experiments to settle design debates, emphasizing human judgment over machine volume.


The irony, as observers noted, is that Outlook still features a "Draft with Copilot" button, potentially encouraging the very behavior Lamanna discourages. Nonetheless, his position reflects a growing concern that AI will flood organizations with low-quality content that still requires human review, negating productivity gains.


## What This Means


Microsoft's disclosure that AI agents now drive 40% of GitHub pull requests signals a structural shift in software development. As agents become the dominant users of enterprise platforms, companies must redesign APIs, user experiences, and coordination tools to serve machine clients. The 14x workload increase at GitHub demonstrates both the scale of agent adoption and the infrastructure challenges it creates. For developers, the transition means less time writing code and more time on system design, testing, and managing agent outputs. Organizations that fail to adapt risk losing agent traffic to competitors with faster, more reliable systems.
